planting.note: Pot in coarse, fast-draining bark mix or mount on a slab; Bellina moth orchid needs warm, humid, shaded conditions year-round and cannot tolerate temperatures below 60F.

directions: Thick, waxy, star-shaped flowers open yellow-green heavily overlaid with rich purple-magenta markings and carry an intense sweet fragrance that peaks in the heat of the afternoon. Unlike the branching sprays of common hybrid moth orchids, Bellina opens just one or two blooms at a time from a short stem, similar in habit to its close relative Phalaenopsis violacea but with a distinctly waxier texture and stronger scent. Native to hot, humid lowland forests in Borneo, it demands consistently warm nights and high humidity to thrive and rebloom reliably.

planting.note: Mount on a bark or cork slab, or pot loosely in coarse bark, for quick root drying between waterings; this species tolerates brighter light than most phalaenopsis but still needs full shade from direct sun.

directions: Flowers are heavily and variably barred in cinnamon-brown to rosy magenta over a white or cream ground, with individual plants showing striking differences in pattern intensity, and carry a light citrusy fragrance. Thick, fleshy, mottled leaves are more leathery than typical moth orchid hybrids, reflecting the species' exposed cliffside habitat in the Philippines. A notable trait is its ability to rebloom repeatedly from the same flower stem over several years if left uncut after flowering, unlike most phalaenopsis grown for a single seasonal bloom cycle.

planting.note: Mount or pot in coarse bark in bright shade; this species tolerates cooler nights than most phalaenopsis, reflecting its native range in the eastern Himalayan foothills.

directions: Slender, slightly twisted golden-yellow sepals and petals are boldly barred with cinnamon-brown stripes, giving each flower a distinctive tiger-like pattern quite different from the round, flat blooms of typical hybrid moth orchids. Fragrant flowers open on arching, pendant sprays in spring and can rebloom from older stems. Ranging from the eastern Himalayas through Vietnam and Hainan, it tolerates cooler winter nights than most tropical phalaenopsis species, making it a good candidate for growers without heated greenhouses.

planting.note: Mount on bark or pot in a small basket to expose the flattened, branching flower stem; never cut the old inflorescence, since new buds continue emerging from it for years.

directions: Named for its flattened, forked flower stem that branches like a deer's antlers, this species produces thick, waxy, star-shaped flowers in yellow-green heavily barred with reddish-brown, opening just one or two at a time in a slow, sequential succession that can continue from the same permanent inflorescence for years. This persistent-stem habit sets it apart from every other phalaenopsis in the dataset, which typically flower from a fresh stem each season. Native across mainland and island Southeast Asia, it tolerates slightly drier conditions between waterings than most moth orchids.

planting.note: Mount on a large slab or basket to accommodate its oversized, pendulous leaves, and grow in deep shade with high humidity; this species is slow to mature and may take several years from a small division to first bloom.

directions: Bears by far the largest leaves in the genus, thick and pendulous, growing up to two feet long on a mature plant, a dramatic contrast to the modest foliage of every other phalaenopsis in the dataset. Short, pendulous flower spikes carry cream to yellow flowers heavily spotted with maroon-red, opening a few at a time over a long season. A slow-growing lowland Borneo species, it needs deep shade and constant humidity to prevent its heavy leaves from scorching or desiccating.

planting.note: Pot in coarse bark and grow with slightly stiffer, more upright leaves held above the pot rather than flat, distinguishing its culture from sprawling phalaenopsis species; keep in deep shade with high humidity.

directions: Waxy flowers show an unusual netted, vein-like pattern of olive-brown lines over a mustard-yellow ground, a distinctive texture unlike the solid bars or spots seen on related species in the dataset. Blooms carry a light fragrance and open successively from a short stem. Discovered relatively recently on the island of Sulawesi, this species grows more upright than most phalaenopsis, holding its stiff leaves above rather than flat against the potting medium.

common_name: Golden Peoker Phalaenopsis (Spotted Yellow Moth Orchid)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio plant in coarse orchid bark mix in bright, indirect light; a widely available commercial hybrid suited to typical windowsill culture.

directions: One of the most widely sold yellow-flowered moth orchid hybrids, producing rounded, flat flowers in bright golden-yellow densely spotted and barred in red-brown, held on branching upright sprays. Bred from spotted species ancestry rather than the plain white or pink parentage behind most mass-market phalaenopsis, it delivers a bolder, more patterned look while retaining the easy, long-lasting bloom habit that made hybrid moth orchids a houseplant staple. Flowers can persist for two to three months under stable indoor conditions.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio plant in coarse orchid bark mix in bright, indirect light; a classic, easy-to-find Taiwanese-bred hybrid well suited to beginner windowsill culture.

directions: A long-established hybrid from the influential Taiwanese 'Brother' breeding line, producing crisp white flowers set off by a compact, contrasting deep red-magenta lip. Multiple branching spikes arise from a single mature plant, each carrying a dozen or more long-lasting flowers over a bloom period that can stretch past two months. Its vigorous growth and reliable rebloom under ordinary indoor light made it one of the influential parents behind many modern white-with-colored-lip phalaenopsis hybrids.

planting.note: Mount on a slab or pot in coarse bark with excellent drainage; give a cool, drier winter rest with bright light to trigger the dense pendulous spring bloom clusters.

directions: Produces dense, pendulous racemes packed with rounded white flowers accented by a fringed, deep golden-yellow lip, the tight cluster resembling a small pineapple hanging beneath the cane. Blooms emerge from nodes along mature, leafy canes in spring, unlike the leafless-cane bloom habit of anosmum already in the dataset. Native from the eastern Himalayas through Indochina at moderate elevation, it appreciates cooler nights and a distinct winter dry rest to flower well.

planting.note: Mount or pot in coarse bark with sharp drainage; provide a brief cooler, drier rest after canes mature to encourage the dense pendulous spring flower clusters.

directions: Closely related to Dendrobium thyrsiflorum and sharing its dense, pendant flower clusters, but blooms are flushed pale rose-lilac to cream rather than pure white, with the same deep yellow-orange fringed lip. Clusters hang from leafy, mature canes in mid-spring and can carry twenty or more flowers per raceme on a well-grown plant. Found across the same eastern Himalaya-to-Indochina range at similar elevations, it requires the same cooler, drier winter rest to initiate strong bloom.

planting.note: Mount on a small slab or grow in a shallow pot of fine bark; its dwarf, trailing stems make it well suited to a bright, cool windowsill rather than a full greenhouse setup.

directions: A dwarf, low-growing species with slender, arching stems rarely more than eight inches long, producing solitary rose-pink flowers with a golden-orange, fringed lip disc that opens along the nodes rather than in terminal clusters. Its compact, trailing habit and tolerance of cooler winter temperatures than most tropical dendrobiums make it one of the easiest species in the genus for a bright windowsill. Stems are semi-deciduous, dropping some leaves before a late-winter bloom flush.

planting.note: Mount on bark or a slab in a spot with bright shade and cool winter nights; more cold-tolerant than most epiphytic dendrobiums, it can summer outdoors well into temperate climates.

directions: Small, fragrant white to pale pink flowers with a faintly spotted lip open along slender, jointed canes in spring, followed by dense new growth through summer. Long cultivated in Japan and China as an ornamental and medicinal plant known as Sekkoku or Chang Shan, it has given rise to hundreds of variegated-leaf cultivars prized in East Asian orchid collecting, distinct from the showier tropical dendrobiums already in the dataset. Native from the Himalayas through Japan and Korea, it withstands cooler nights than most epiphytic orchids in cultivation.

common_name: Golden Bells Dendrobium (Lindleyi Orchid, Aggregatum Orchid)

planting.note: Mount on bark or wood rather than potting, since the short, clumping pseudobulbs and pendulous flower clusters need to hang freely; give a distinct cooler, drier winter rest to trigger heavy spring bloom.

directions: Short, clustered pseudobulbs send out dense, pendulous clusters of small, rounded, bright golden-yellow flowers with a fragrance often described as citrusy or honey-like. Mature clumps bloom explosively in spring, with dozens of flower clusters opening within a week or two of each other, a far showier and more compact display than the tall canes of most dendrobiums in the dataset. Widespread from the Himalayas through Southeast Asia, it is commonly sold under its older synonym Dendrobium aggregatum.

planting.note: Mount on a slab or hang in a basket with minimal medium; give a hard winter dry rest with reduced water once leaves drop, matching the culture of other deciduous cane dendrobiums.

directions: Deciduous canes, shorter and stouter than those of the related Dendrobium anosmum already in the dataset, lose their leaves in the dry season before bursting into bloom along their full length. Rounded, fragrant rose-purple flowers feature a darker maroon blotch in the throat, opening in pairs at each node. Native to the hills of Myanmar, Thailand, and Laos, it requires the same firm winter rest and reduced watering as anosmum to flower reliably rather than produce keikis.

common_name: Berry Oda Dendrobium (Dark Purple Hard-Cane Orchid)

planting.note: Pot in coarse bark with a stake to support the tall, upright canes; grow in warm, bright, humid conditions year-round, since this hard-cane hybrid does not take a leaf-dropping dry rest like the soft-cane species in the dataset.

directions: A classic Hawaiian-bred hard-cane hybrid producing tall, upright canes topped with sprays of deep wine-purple to near-black velvety flowers, a striking contrast to the paler nobile-type and antelope-type dendrobiums already represented in the dataset. Long-lasting flower sprays have made it a longtime favorite for cut-flower and lei arrangements in Hawaii. Unlike deciduous soft-cane species, it stays evergreen year-round and does not require a leafless winter rest to bloom.
sources: University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources

planting.note: Mount on a slab or pot loosely in coarse bark; this bifoliate species tolerates brighter light and slightly less water between waterings than the unifoliate Cattleyas already in the dataset.

directions: Bifoliate, coastal Brazilian species bearing lavender-pink sepals and petals around a frilled, magenta-purple lip, with some naturally occurring color forms showing a nearly white flower splashed only on the lip. Two leaves per pseudobulb and a more compact, clustering growth habit distinguish it from the single-leafed Cattleya species already in the dataset. Blooms open in late spring to summer, opposite the winter-flowering season typical of trianae and percivaliana.

planting.note: Mount on a cork or tree-fern slab to accommodate its creeping rhizome, and grow in bright light with good air movement; the dwarf, sprawling habit does not suit a standard pot.

directions: Unusual among Cattleyas for its dwarf, creeping rhizome that spreads sideways along a mount rather than clumping upright, and for its heavily spotted flowers: olive to yellow-green sepals and petals densely marked with maroon-purple blotches, set off by a vivid rose-purple lip. Intensely fragrant blooms open singly or in pairs from short, thick pseudobulbs. Native to rocky, sun-exposed outcrops in Bahia, Brazil, it tolerates and needs brighter light than most shade-loving Cattleyas.

planting.note: Mount on a slab or pot in coarse bark; this compact unifoliate species can flower more than once a year under bright, consistent conditions rather than on a single seasonal cycle.

directions: A compact, unifoliate species from the coastal restinga and mangrove-edge habitats of Brazil, producing soft olive to buff-yellow flowers with a slender, tubular lip lined in maroon inside its throat. Unlike many Cattleya species that bloom on a single annual cycle, this species can flower more than once a year under warm, bright, consistent conditions. Its smaller stature and unusual muted flower color make it a popular choice for hybridizing compact, novelty-colored Cattleya crosses.

planting.note: Mount on a slab or pot in coarse bark in bright light; give a brief cooler, drier rest in autumn to encourage on-time flowering around the winter holidays.

directions: Compact, unifoliate species bearing rosy-lavender flowers with a dramatically darker lip marked by a deep maroon throat streaked in gold, blooming reliably around the winter holidays in its native Venezuelan and Colombian cloud forests. It flowers a few weeks earlier in the season and shows a more richly colored throat blotch than the similarly winter-blooming Cattleya trianae already in the dataset. A cool, brief autumn rest with reduced water helps synchronize its bloom with the December holiday season it is named for.

planting.note: Pot in coarse bark with excellent drainage and provide strong, bright light; this species is notoriously slower and more demanding to establish than most Cattleyas, needing several years of steady growth before its first bloom.

directions: Known as the Queen Cattleya for its unusually rich coloring: golden-yellow petals and sepals surrounding a broad, velvety crimson lip intricately veined in gold. One of the most historically prized species in Cattleya breeding, it contributed the golden and gold-veined coloring seen in countless modern hybrids. Native to Costa Rica and Colombia, it demands stronger light and sharper drainage than most Cattleyas in the dataset, and is generally considered one of the more challenging species to grow well.

planting.note: Pot in a large basket or coarse bark to support its sizeable pseudobulbs, and provide sturdy stakes for the heavy summer flowers; this species needs more root and pot space than most Cattleyas in the dataset.

directions: Produces some of the largest flowers in the entire genus, often exceeding eight inches across, in soft rose-lavender with a dramatically frilled, crimson-purple lip marked with a golden throat. Unlike the winter- and fall-blooming Cattleya species already in the dataset, this Colombian species flowers in mid-summer, on large, robust pseudobulbs that need generous pot space to develop fully. Long known in cultivation under its older synonym Cattleya gigas, it remains one of the most dramatic species used in large-flowered Cattleya hybridizing.

planting.note: Pot in coarse bark in bright, filtered light; a vigorous, easy-to-grow classic hybrid well suited to a sunny patio or bright greenhouse bench.

directions: A long-established English-bred white Cattleya hybrid producing crisp, pure white flowers with a bright yellow-orange throat, historically important as one of the standard white-flowered corsage orchids of the mid-20th century cut-flower trade. Vigorous and free-flowering compared to many species Cattleyas, it produces multiple flowers per spike on well-grown plants. Its clean color combination and reliable performance have kept it in commercial production and hobbyist collections for decades.

planting.note: Mount on a small slab or grow in a shallow basket of fine bark; this miniature cloud-forest species prefers cooler, more humid conditions and finer, faster-draining medium than the larger Oncidium species in the dataset.

directions: A dwarf, cloud-forest species from Colombia and Costa Rica producing dense, rounded, pendant clusters of small, deep golden-yellow flowers with a rich honey-like fragrance strongest on cool mornings. Its miniature scale, staying well under a foot tall, contrasts sharply with the much larger sphacelatum and varicosum already in the dataset. Blooms open in fall to winter on mature clumps grown in bright, humid, moderately cool conditions.

planting.note: Mount on a slab or pot in coarse, fast-draining bark; a warm-growing, easy Brazilian species tolerant of bright light and brief drying out between waterings.

directions: Wiry, zig-zagging flower stems give this Brazilian species its species name and branch into airy sprays of small, bright yellow flowers barred in reddish-brown, whose fluttering lips inspired the common 'dancing doll' nickname shared across several Oncidium-alliance species. Compact, clustering pseudobulbs make it an easy, warm-tolerant grower well suited to bright outdoor conditions in frost-free climates. Blooms typically appear in late summer to fall on well-established clumps.

common_name: Sweet Sugar Oncidium (Fragrant Miniature Dancing Lady)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio plant in coarse, fast-draining bark mix in bright, indirect light; a compact, easy-flowering miniature suited to windowsill culture.

directions: A compact Oncidium-alliance hybrid bred as a fragrant miniature, producing branching sprays of small yellow-brown flowers with a pronounced, sweet candy-like scent noticeable across a room. Its small stature and free-flowering habit make it a popular novelty for growers with limited windowsill or shelf space compared to the larger sphacelatum and varicosum already in the dataset. Blooms readily under bright indoor light and can flower more than once per year on a vigorous clump.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio plant in coarse bark mix in bright, indirect light; a vigorous, heavy-blooming hybrid widely grown commercially for cut flowers.

directions: One of the most commercially important Oncidium hybrids in the cut-flower trade, prized for tall, branching sprays densely packed with bright yellow flowers marked red-brown at the base of the lip. Its exceptional vigor, floriferousness, and long vase life have made it a mainstay of Taiwan's export cut-flower industry for decades. Easier and faster to bring into flower than most species Oncidiums, it also performs well as a houseplant given bright light and regular feeding.

planting.note: Pot in coarse bark with sturdy support for the tall flower spikes; this high-elevation Andean species tolerates cooler nights than the lowland Oncidium species already in the dataset.

directions: Thick, deeply ridged pseudobulbs send up tall, upright spikes of golden-yellow flowers spotted with red-brown, blooming in winter to spring. Native to high-elevation cloud forests in Peru and Ecuador, it tolerates and even prefers cooler nighttime temperatures than the lowland sphacelatum and varicosum already represented in the dataset. Its sturdy, deeply grooved pseudobulbs and tall spikes make it a distinct, cold-hardier alternative among the larger Oncidium species grown for cut flowers or greenhouse display.
